prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "STARBUCKS CORP" (ticker SBUX), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SBUX", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Starbucks Corporation
result.industry: Specialty coffee retail and branded coffee products
markets: Coffeehouses and specialty coffee drinks (US and international)
Licensed Starbucks stores (airports, grocery, China joint venture)
Packaged coffee, pods and ready-to-drink beverages (Channel Development)

mission.statement: To be the premier purveyor of the finest coffee in the world, inspiring and nurturing the human spirit — one person, one cup and one neighborhood at a time.
mission.plain: Serve the best coffee in the world and make each visit a warm, human moment in every neighbourhood.

about.plain: Starbucks runs coffee shops all over the world where people buy coffee, tea, cold drinks and snacks. It owns about a third of its 41,304 shops and lets partners run the rest using the Starbucks name. It also sells bagged coffee, coffee pods and bottled drinks in supermarkets through partners like Nestlé and PepsiCo. Many customers order ahead on its phone app and earn free drinks.
about.customers: Everyday people grabbing a coffee or snack, mostly in the US and also in dozens of other countries.
about.everyday: The green mermaid cup that people carry to work or school, and the app many use to order before they arrive.

money.plain: drinks and food sold in its own stores
coffee, food and fees from partner-run Starbucks shops
bagged coffee, pods and bottled drinks in shops

money.part: China joint venture with Boyu Capital
money.plain: royalties and a 40% share of China's 8,000+ stores

result.summary: Starbucks has a real but narrowing advantage: the world's best-known coffee brand, 41,304 stores and a 35.6 million-member US Rewards programme give it scale no other coffeehouse matches. The edge has weakened as cheaper, faster rivals such as Luckin took share in China (Euromonitor: 34% in 2019 to 14% in 2024) and US traffic fell in 2024-25, but the Back to Starbucks turnaround returned US comparable sales to +7.9% in Q3 FY2026.

pricingPower.evidence: Years of price rises pushed ticket up while traffic fell: in FY2025 North America comparable sales were -2% with transactions -4% and ticket +2%. After the turnaround, Q3 FY2026 US comps rose 7.9% with both transactions (+4.2%) and ticket (+3.6%) growing, showing customers will pay premium prices when service and experience are good.

moats.evidence: Starbucks is the world's most recognised coffeehouse brand, a Fortune World's Most Admired Companies All-Star (rank 28), and its name supports premium-priced packaged coffee sold by Nestlé and ready-to-drink beverages sold with PepsiCo.
Rewards points and stored-value balances give a mild reason to stay (US 90-day active members reached a record 35.6 million in 2026), but a customer can buy coffee elsewhere at no cost.
The app and loyalty programme get better with more data but do not become more valuable to one customer because others use them.
With $37,184.4M of FY2025 revenue and 40,990 stores it has buying, roasting and marketing scale, but value chains like Luckin and McDonald's McCafé sell coffee far more cheaply.
Coffee retail has low barriers to entry and thousands of independent shops and chains; dense store networks deter some entrants but not well-funded rivals.
Starbucks is the incumbent being counter-positioned against by cheaper app-only chains (Luckin, Cotti) and drive-thru chains (Dutch Bros).
Its global sourcing, roasting and supply chain plus the mobile order and pay system are hard to replicate at its scale, although 2024's slow mobile-order service showed execution can slip.
Prime store locations and long-term partnerships (Nestlé Global Coffee Alliance, PepsiCo North American Coffee Partnership) help, but no input is truly exclusive.

customers.evidence: US 90-day active Starbucks Rewards membership grew 4% to a record 35.6 million in 2026, and transactions rose 4.2% in US stores in Q3 FY2026 after falling 4% in FY2025, showing loyalty recovered once service improved.

talent.evidence: Starbucks offers benefits rare in restaurants (healthcare, ASU online degree, stock grants) and is a Fortune Most Admired All-Star, but about 550 US stores unionised with Starbucks Workers United, which struck from November 13, 2025 without a first contract, and corporate staff faced layoffs in 2025.

product.evidence: Starbucks is the default premium coffeehouse with the widest store network and a leading mobile-ordering app, but its coffee is not clearly best in class against specialty roasters, and cheaper rivals match it on convenience.

competitors.name: Luckin Coffee
competitors.note: China's largest coffee chain by store count, competing on low prices and app-only pickup; also expanding abroad, including Singapore and the US.

competitors.name: Dunkin' (Inspire Brands)
competitors.note: Private US coffee-and-breakfast chain competing on value and drive-thru.

competitors.name: Dutch Bros
competitors.note: Fast-growing US drive-thru drinks chain popular with younger customers.

competitors.name: McDonald's (McCafé)
competitors.note: Cheap coffee and breakfast at tens of thousands of restaurants worldwide; pushing into specialty drinks.

competitors.name: Restaurant Brands International (Tim Hortons)
competitors.note: Tim Hortons leads coffee in Canada and is expanding in China and Asia.

competitors.name: Cotti Coffee
competitors.note: Private Chinese discount coffee chain founded by Luckin's founders.

competitors.name: Costa Coffee (The Coca-Cola Company)
competitors.note: UK-based coffeehouse chain and Costa Express machines in the UK, Europe and China.

competitors.name: Mixue Group
competitors.note: Huge low-price tea and coffee (Lucky Cup) chain in China and Southeast Asia.

competitors.name: Nestlé (Nescafé, Nespresso, Blue Bottle)
competitors.note: Largest packaged coffee company; also Starbucks' partner selling Starbucks packaged coffee outside its stores.

competitors.name: JDE Peet's (Peet's Coffee)
competitors.note: Peet's coffeehouses in the US and China and packaged coffee brands in grocery.

competitors.name: Keurig Dr Pepper
competitors.note: K-Cup pods and home brewers competing for at-home coffee.

competitors.name: Chagee
competitors.note: Premium Chinese tea-house chain competing for the same urban daily-drink spend.

competitors.name: Krispy Kreme
competitors.note: Doughnut-and-coffee shops and grocery doughnut cases.

competitors.name: Panera Bread (JAB Holding)
competitors.note: Private bakery-cafe chain with a coffee subscription competing for breakfast visits.

competitors.name: Independent specialty coffee shops and roasters
competitors.note: Thousands of local cafes and premium chains such as Blue Bottle and Philz competing on quality and atmosphere.

threats: Low-price app-based chains (Luckin, Cotti, Mixue's Lucky Cup) taking share in China and expanding abroad, including Luckin's first stores abroad
US traffic sensitivity to high prices: FY2025 North America transactions fell 4% before the turnaround
Labour costs and unresolved first-contract talks with Starbucks Workers United (about 550 unionised stores, strike from November 13, 2025)
Coffee bean price swings and tariffs on imported coffee
Reduced control of the China business after selling 60% to Boyu Capital in 2026
Execution risk and high spending in the Back to Starbucks turnaround (restructuring and impairments of $892.0M in FY2025 and $415.8M in the first nine months of FY2026)

ceo.name: Brian Niccol
ceo.background: Former Chipotle CEO (2018-2024) and Taco Bell CEO; began at Procter & Gamble; BS Miami University, MBA University of Chicago

c1.evidence: Coffeehouses are a mature industry; Starbucks' revenue grew only 2.8% in FY2025 and it is the leader of an established, not emerging, market.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Starbucks for its brand, consistent drinks, store density and the Rewards app (35.6M US active members), but cheaper rivals such as Luckin have copied the app-ordering model, cutting its China share from 34% (2019) to 14% (2024).

c3.evidence: Starbucks is a household name and the default premium coffeehouse in the US with 16,933 stores, though many customers recommend it more for convenience than for the coffee itself.

c4.evidence: Its mission to inspire and nurture the human spirit 'one person, one cup and one neighborhood at a time' is restated often and Niccol's Back to Starbucks plan centres on the coffeehouse experience, but the mission matters to customers' daily routine rather than changing the world.

c6.evidence: “expensive, convenient, iconic”: people see Starbucks as a familiar, premium everyday treat, mostly positive but with frequent complaints about price, sweet drinks and wait times.

c7.evidence: Global coffee consumption is large and growing slowly, with faster growth in China and cold drinks, but it is not a high-growth secular trend like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: Room remains in international markets (22,933 international stores) and through the China joint venture's goal of up to 20,000 outlets, but the brand is tied to coffee and adjacent food.

m1.evidence: Brian Niccol has a clear operational vision ('Back to Starbucks', becoming 'the world's greatest customer service company'), focused on fixing the core rather than a new future.

m2.evidence: Niccol is not a founder but has acted decisively and hands-on (menu cuts, Green Apron service model, new store staffing); founder Howard Schultz no longer runs the company.

m4.evidence: His plan invested in store staffing and service for customers, but cut about 1,100 corporate roles in 2025 and has not yet reached a contract with unionised baristas.

m5.evidence: Niccol is rebuilding a service culture after Chipotle, where he oversaw digital ordering and new products, but Starbucks' recent innovation is mostly menu and service changes.

m6.evidence: Niccol is deeply involved in stores and menus but is a marketer by background (Procter & Gamble, MBA), not an engineer.

m7.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way beyond the company's stated partner, farmer and community promises.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Brian Niccol at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: Niccol is respected as a turnaround operator but keeps a low-key, conventional public profile.

m9.evidence: At Chipotle (2018-2024) he grew revenue strongly and widened margins, and at Starbucks US comparable sales went from -2% in FY2025 to +7.9% in Q3 FY2026.

m10.evidence: Starbucks is not known for frugality, and Niccol's offer letter allowed him to commute from California using the corporate aircraft.

c10.evidence: It serves millions of people a day in dozens of countries and supports coffee farmers, but it sells an affordable treat rather than solving a major problem.

p2.evidence: Running coffee shops at scale is operationally demanding but not technologically hard or critical to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2020 ($23,518.0M) to FY2025 ($37,184.4M), though growth slowed to 0.6% in FY2024 and 2.8% in FY2025.

f2.evidence: Operating margin fell from 16.8% in FY2021 to 7.9% in FY2025 as labour costs, restructuring ($892.0M) and impairments rose.

f3.evidence: Debt of $13,278.6M far exceeds cash and short-term investments of $3,610.3M (June 28, 2026), and shareholders' equity is negative at -$7,674.3M.

f4.evidence: Operating income fell from $4,872.1M in FY2021 to $2,936.6M in FY2025, and operating cash flow fell from $5,989.1M to $4,747.5M.

v1.evidence: Starbucks is the most convenient premium coffee choice, but many people prefer cheaper (Dunkin', McCafé, Luckin) or higher-quality independent coffee, so it is not clearly the best.

v2.evidence: It is a Fortune World's Most Admired Companies All-Star (rank 28) known for barista benefits, but labour disputes with Starbucks Workers United hurt its reputation as an employer.

c5.evidence: Regulars would miss their daily ritual, meeting place and app, but other coffee chains would quickly fill the gap.
